title: A voice recorded for 80 years. A career that started with a knee injury. September 28, 2026.
excerpt: From a singer whose recordings outlasted every era she sang through to a factory turning wasted power into fuel, September 28's five stories share one thread: nothing here was recognized quickly - it was recognized after decades of showing up.
bodyHtml:
Every story today took years, sometimes decades, before the recognition caught up to the work - a voice recorded across generations before an anniversary made people count them, a climate signal tracked for years before a prize named it, a physics career built since the 1980s before an academy inducted it, a night spent on a railway platform before a district was handed to run, and a factory habit of wasting power before someone decided to stop.

September 28, 1929: a voice was born in Indore that would become the soundtrack of a nation

Lata Mangeshkar was born on September 28, 1929, in Indore, British India. She began playback singing in the 1940s, and her 1962 rendition of 'Ae Mere Watan Ke Logo' became a de facto national anthem after the war with China. Known as the 'Swar Kokila,' she recorded over 2,000 film songs across 8 decades until shortly before her death in 2022, and received the Bharat Ratna in 2001, India's highest civilian honor, along with the Padma Vibhushan and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award.

He spent years measuring a warming ocean. The world's largest Earth science society just gave him its top communications honor

Roxy Mathew Koll, a climate scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune, won the American Geophysical Union's 2026 Climate Communications Prize - one of only 43 AGU honors awarded globally this year, carrying a $25,000 award. His research documented how a warming Indian Ocean is reshaping monsoons, cyclones and marine heatwaves across South Asia. A second Indian scientist, Neelima Satyam of IIT-Indore, was named in the same 2026 cohort for the Devendra Lal Memorial Medal.

He left IIT Bombay for a PhD in America. In 2026, one of the world's oldest honor societies inducted him

Nitin Samarth was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences' 2026 class, in its Mathematical and Physical Sciences section - a society founded in 1780. He holds the Verne M. Willaman Professorship of Physics at Penn State and has published roughly 300 papers on spin coherence in semiconductors and topological insulators, per Penn State's own announcement. His path ran from a B.S. at IIT Bombay in 1980, to a PhD at Purdue, to over a decade leading Penn State's Physics Department.

He slept on a railway platform to afford weekend classes. He now runs a district as an IAS officer

M. Sivaguru Prabakaran grew up in a farming family in Tamil Nadu, where his father struggled with unemployment. He worked as a sawmill operator and did farm labour to fund his own education, while his mother and sister wove bamboo baskets at night to support the household. While attending weekend engineering classes in Vellore, he slept on the platforms of St. Thomas Mount railway station. He went on to complete an M.Tech from IIT Madras, then cleared the UPSC Civil Services exam on his fourth attempt with All India Rank 101, becoming an IAS officer.

Maruti Suzuki just started making its own hydrogen - from power it used to waste

On September 24, 2026, Maruti Suzuki commissioned its first green hydrogen electrolyser plant, a 300 kW facility at its Manesar factory in Haryana. The plant uses surplus solar power generated on factory holidays - power that would otherwise go unused - to split water into hydrogen, which is then blended with natural gas as manufacturing fuel. The pilot supports India's National Green Hydrogen Mission, with plans to scale the approach to other plants in Haryana and Gujarat.

Five stories, one thread: a voice that took eight decades to fully register as a nation's soundtrack, a climate signal that took years of patient measurement before it earned a prize, a physics career that took over four decades from an IIT Bombay classroom to induction into a 246-year-old academy, a railway platform that had to be slept on before a district could be run, and a factory that had to notice its own waste before it could turn it into fuel. Nothing here was an overnight result. Everything here was a long habit that eventually got noticed.
